reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Classically defined by the triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait skin macules, and autonomous endocrine hyperfunction, though not all features are always present
Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty is the most common endocrine manifestation, frequently the presenting problem in young girls
The café-au-lait patches typically have irregular jagged borders (often likened to the coast of Maine) and tend to follow the midline
Fibrous dysplasia weakens bone and can cause pain, deformity, and pathological fractures, and skull base involvement may compress cranial nerves
Additional autonomous endocrinopathies include hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, and Cushing syndrome in infancy
Renal phosphate wasting from excess FGF23 may produce hypophosphataemia and contribute to bone disease
The disorder is caused by a post-zygotic activating GNAS mutation, so it is mosaic and never inherited, with features reflecting the distribution of affected cells
Because endocrine overactivity is autonomous, treatment targets hormone excess at the gland or peripheral level rather than the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
reference.pathophysiology: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a somatic, post-zygotic activating mutation of GNAS encoding the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit. Constitutive activation of this signalling pathway causes cyclic AMP-dependent hormone-secreting cells to function autonomously, independent of normal trophic control, producing precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, GH excess, or hypercortisolism. In bone, the mutation drives replacement of normal marrow and trabeculae with fibrous tissue (fibrous dysplasia), while in skin it produces melanocytic café-au-lait pigmentation. Because the mutation occurs after conception, the syndrome is mosaic, and the clinical pattern depends on which tissues carry the mutant clone.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of childhood hyperthyroidism such as Graves disease
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other causes of virilisation
additionalInvestigations: Sex steroid levels with suppressed gonadotropins to confirm peripheral precocious puberty
Thyroid function tests and thyroid ultrasound
IGF-1 and growth hormone assessment for acromegaly/gigantism
Serum phosphate and FGF23 for renal phosphate wasting
Skeletal survey or bone scan to map fibrous dysplasia
Cortisol studies where infantile Cushing syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Skull base fibrous dysplasia causing visual loss, hearing loss, or cranial nerve compression
Pathological fractures or severe progressive bone deformity
Infantile Cushing syndrome, which can be life-threatening and needs urgent evaluation
Severe hyperthyroidism or high-output complications from autonomous glandular overactivity
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the extent of skeletal disease and the number of endocrinopathies; many patients have manageable disease, but extensive fibrous dysplasia can cause chronic disability, and severe neonatal endocrine involvement carries higher risk.
pitfalls: Treating precocious puberty as central and using GnRH analogues, which are ineffective for the peripheral mechanism
Overlooking additional autonomous endocrinopathies once one is found
Missing craniofacial fibrous dysplasia threatening vision or hearing
Attributing café-au-lait macules solely to neurofibromatosis
Ignoring hypophosphataemia as a contributor to bone fragility
